title: Hash set
short: Answer "have I seen this?" in one step.
what: A hash set is a bag of unique values. Adding a value, removing it, or asking whether it is there each take one step on average, however many values you store. It is a hash map with keys and no values. In Python it is the set.
analogy: A guest list at the door. The bouncer checks your name against the list at a glance, and the same name can't be on it twice.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: Task: find the first number that appears twice. We walk the list once and keep a set called seen.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: 3: is 3 in seen? No, so add it.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: 1: not in seen. Add it. The check is one step, not a loop over everything before it.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: 4: not in seen either. Add it.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: 1 again. 1 in seen is True, so 1 is the first repeat. 4 cheap checks instead of comparing every pair.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: set(nums) keeps one copy of each value: 6 numbers in, 5 out. Fewer means the list had a repeat.

when: Have I seen this value before?
Does the list contain a duplicate?
What do two lists have in common?
python:
nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9]
seen = set()
for x in nums:
    if x in seen:
        print("first repeat:", x)
        break
    seen.add(x)
print(sorted(set(nums)))
print(len(set(nums)) < len(nums))
a, b = {1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 4}
print(a & b, a | b, a - b)
cost: Check if a value is in it
watch: {} is an empty dict, not a set. Write set().
A set has no order and no index. Sort it if you need order.
Values must be unchangeable: numbers, strings, tuples. A list can't go in a set.
